newsitem.title: UK: UK's battered Conservatives vote for new leader.
newsitem.headline: UK's battered Conservatives vote for new leader.

text.p: Conservative members of parliament started voting on Thursday for a new leader to succeed John Major after a bitter contest that has magnified the main opposition party's already deep divisions over Europe.
The result of the ballot, to be decided by the 164 Conservative MPs who survived the May 1 election rout at the hands of Tony Blair's Labour party, is too close to call.

But the camps of the two candidates, former finance minister Kenneth Clarke and ex-Welsh secretary William Hague, exuded confidence as voting got under way in a committee room at the House of Commons. The result is due shortly after 1600 GMT.
"I never predict results but things are looking good," said John Redwood, who has been promised the plum job of finance spokesman if Clarke wins.

Redwood, a messianic opponent of closer European integration, threw the race into turmoil on Wednesday by linking up with Clarke, a hate figure for Conservative Euro-sceptics because of his defence of Britain's place in Europe.

Redwood's move was denounced by Conservative right-wingers afraid it would scupper Hague's chances and open the door to Clarke, whom they blame for the May 1 election defeat because he refused to rule out joining Europe's planned single currency.
Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher called it an alliance of incredible opposites.
"Very strange bedfellows" was the headline in The Independent newspaper.

"A marriage made in the Tory party's hell" was the headline of an article by Charles Moore, right-wing editor of the Daily Telegraph, who said he had never seen an odder sight in British politics than Redwood and Clarke sharing the same stage.
"Perhaps the Conservatives no longer believe that there is any possibility of agreement. Perhaps they are really no more than a number of factions...

"If so, none of them will have a seat at the next election, and the most enduring and successful political party in the history of the world will have moved from zenith to extinction in a single decade," he wrote.

But Clarke defended his partnership and said the Conservatives needed to emulate Blair, who has united Labour's factions by means of a strong alliance with John Prescott, his deputy from the opposite, left wing of the party.

"Why aren't the Labour party kicking pieces out of each other? It is because the Labour party had more sense and we had less sense and we spent the last three years arguing with each other," Clarke told BBC radio on Thursday.

"We've been pointing at Prescott alongside Blair for the last three or four years. If you listen to the critics of the agreement that I entered into with John Redwood yesterday, Blair made a terrible mistake -- he should have spent his time throwing John Prescott out.
Hague mocked the Clarke-Redwood alliance as a deal, not a solution, and critics said the two men's agreement to disagree over Europe was a recipe for disaster.
But Clarke said the party had to restore unity if it was serious about regaining power at the next election.
"By 2002 there has not got to be a serious whisker between any leading members of the Conservative Party if we are to have the slightest chance of success," he said.
